full_judgment: 4. In the instant case the plaintiff claimed tenancy right in the suit land under Bibhuti Bushan and not under his sons whose names are subsequently recorded in the respective khatian and who were impleaded as defendants 1 and 2 in the suit by the plaintiff himself. The plaintiff in order to prove the settlement could not produce any documentary evidence, such as patta or kabulyat but Dakhilas of these nature, which are private documents would not carry with it any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of an entry in the record of right under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The said dakhilas thus need "to be proved, out of necessity by person who wishes the court to believe in the existence of these papers to the satisfaction of the court by any of the ways that would be considered by the Court of Law sufficient to prove a document as the Evidence Act does not provide any particular mode of proving a document. It can be proved by calling the scribe, and in case the signature of the executant was disputed, by comparing the disputed signature with other proved signature of the executant and by taking the opinion of a handwriting expert and in the case of a document need to be attested by examing at least one of the attesting witness. In the instant case the documents or dakhilas, when challenged by the opposite parties to be a concocted document, need be proved by producing the scribe as a witness and also the executant to prove that he had in fact signed the document as an employee under the Zamindar and had the authority granted by Landlord to grant such a receipt and finally by producing the counter-foil of those dakhilas. In the instant case nothing of that nature had been done. No counterfoil had been produced neither the scribe nor the executant deposed in favour of the dakhila. The Courts below on an examination of those documents found those to be of recent origin and therefore of no legal value. The question whether a document is a genuine document or not is essentially a question of fact and a finding of fact to that effect need not to be interfered with by this court in revisional jurisdiction unless it could be shown that the finding was not warranted by the evidence on record which would give rise to a question of legality. In the instant case the finding of fact to the effect that the documents were of recent origin and that the plaintiff could not prove his title to the suit land by other document of title, do not seem to have been arrived at by causing any error of law or which was not warranted by the evidence on record. Hence the contention of the learned Advocate that the court below committed an error in this regard cannot be sustained.
